stories.headline: AUGUST CPI COMES IN HOT, FED HIKE ODDS JUMP TO 90%
stories.body: The August CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month and 3.4% year-over-year, matching headline estimates, but core CPI (ex-food and energy) climbed 0.3%, slightly above forecast. CME FedWatch now prices roughly a 90% probability of a quarter-point hike at next week's FOMC meeting, up from about 70% before the report.
stories.explain: Core CPI strips out volatile food and energy prices to isolate underlying, stickier inflation trends, so a hotter-than-expected core print tells the Fed that price pressure isn't just a passthrough from oil or food shocks. Markets price rate decisions off the fed funds futures curve, and a small miss on core can swing implied probabilities sharply when the market was already split. That's why a beat of just a tenth of a point moved hike odds by 20 percentage points in a single session.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD CLIMBS TO 4.97%, WITHIN STRIKING DISTANCE OF 5%
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.97%, its highest level since 2023, capping a week in which it climbed nearly 20 basis points amid a broader global bond selloff. Today's CPI print added roughly 3 basis points on top of Thursday's 11-basis-point jump triggered by a hot PPI reading.
stories.explain: Long-term yields reflect both the expected path of short-term rates and a term premium investors demand for holding duration risk over a longer horizon, and both components have been rising together this week as hike odds increase and investors demand more compensation for holding bonds through a period of resurgent inflation. A 10-year yield near 5% directly raises the discount rate used to value future corporate cash flows, which is why equity investors watch this level as a valuation ceiling for the broader market, not just a bond-market curiosity.

stories.headline: OIL EASES OFF $104 HIGH AS IRAN SIGNALS HORMUZ DIPLOMACY
stories.body: WTI crude fell 3.13% to roughly $100 a barrel Friday after touching a spring high near $104 on Thursday, as Iranian state media said Tehran would meet Gulf states in Oman to discuss the Strait of Hormuz. Even with the pullback, WTI is still up 9.4% for the week amid the broader escalation in the region.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz carries roughly a fifth of global oil supply, so even a diplomatic signal that transit risk might ease can knock several dollars off the price without any actual barrel of oil changing hands — markets are pricing the probability of disruption, not just current flows. That same risk premium is why the weekly gain of 9.4% persists even after Friday's retreat: traders are unwilling to fully unwind the hedge until the underlying tension is resolved, not just talked about.

stories.headline: STOCKS SNAP FOUR-DAY SKID DESPITE HAWKISH SETUP
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.86% to 7,657 and the Nasdaq-100 gained 0.91% to 29,368, both halting a four-session losing streak, as easing oil prices offset a CPI report that all but locked in a Fed rate hike next week. Gold still added 1.04% to $4,390 even as the dollar index dipped 0.05% to 99.10.
stories.explain: A rate hike that is fully priced in before it happens tends to do less damage to risk assets than a surprise, because markets have already spent the days beforehand repricing valuations and positioning around it — the CPI report mostly confirmed what Thursday's PPI print had already signaled. That's why stocks could rally on a day when hike odds jumped to 90%: the marginal news was the retreat in oil, not the inflation data itself, since the oil move directly changes the outlook for both consumer spending and future inflation prints.

stories.headline: ORACLE JUMPS AS CLOUD REVENUE SURGES 62%, GUIDANCE RAISED
stories.body: Oracle reported fiscal Q1 adjusted EPS of $1.92 on revenue of $19.35 billion, both ahead of Street estimates, as cloud infrastructure revenue soared 62% to $11.61 billion. The company raised its full-year EPS guidance to $8.10 and its revenue outlook to roughly $90 billion, sending shares sharply higher.
stories.explain: Oracle's cloud infrastructure backlog is one of the market's cleanest proxies for hyperscaler AI capital spending, so a 62% growth rate combined with raised full-year guidance reassures investors that enterprise AI demand is durable rather than front-loaded. That reassurance matters more on a day when macro data (hot CPI, near-5% yields) would otherwise argue for compressing high-multiple growth stocks, showing how a strong idiosyncratic result can decouple a single name from top-down macro pressure.

stories.headline: ST. JOHN'S FORWARD BABACAR SANE GRANTED TEMPORARY ELIGIBILITY VIA COURT ORDER
stories.body: A New York Supreme Court judge issued a temporary restraining order allowing St. John's forward Babacar Sane to practice and work out with the Red Storm, after the NCAA denied his reinstatement application over prior G-League experience (112 games, 8.6 ppg for G League Ignite and two D-League affiliates). The order does not guarantee playing eligibility; a hearing set for October 1 will decide whether Sane can suit up for the 2026-27 season.

stories.headline: SUNS CENTER MARK WILLIAMS OUT EXTENDED TIME AFTER SHOULDER SURGERY
stories.body: Phoenix center Mark Williams underwent surgery Thursday to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder, suffered during an offseason workout, and will miss extended time. The injury news lands amid a quiet stretch of roster moves, with DeMar DeRozan (Nuggets) and Ben Simmons (Clippers) both signing one-year deals this week as teams round out camp rosters ahead of the Oct. 24 tip-off.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS SURVIVE WITHOUT DARNOLD, TOP PATRIOTS 13-10 IN SUPER BOWL REMATCH
stories.body: Backup Drew Lock led Seattle to a 13-10 win over New England in the season-opening Kickoff Game, a rematch of Super Bowl LX, after starter Sam Darnold exited with a hip injury on Seattle's first drive. Darnold is expected to miss Week 2; Patriots QB Drake Maye threw three interceptions in the loss, and WR A.J. Brown (ankle) didn't play.

stories.headline: BAYLOR'S DJ LAGWAY RULED OUT FOR WEEK 2 WITH ANKLE SPRAIN
stories.body: Baylor quarterback DJ Lagway will not play Saturday against Prairie View A&M after spraining his ankle in the Bears' 17-16 Week 1 loss to Auburn, where he was carried to the locker room at halftime before returning to nearly rally Baylor to a win. Backup Nate Bennett will start in Waco as Lagway is considered day-to-day.

sports.detail: No. 17 Washington beat Washington State 24-10 in the Apple Cup season opener Sept. 6; QB Demond Williams Jr. threw for 268 yards and a touchdown. Next: hosts Utah State, Saturday, Sept. 12.

Added Texas Tech transfer LeJuan Watts (11.8 ppg, 6.0 reb last season) and Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno as the roster rebuild continues under Danny Sprinkle, who also added a new assistant coach this offseason.
Beat the Patriots 13-10 in the Super Bowl LX rematch to open the season 1-0, but starter Sam Darnold left with a hip injury and is expected to miss Week 2; Drew Lock will likely start in his place.

Fresh off a franchise-best 60-22 season and a No. 1 seed in the East, Detroit still hasn't re-signed restricted free agent center Jalen Duren with training camp three weeks away; backup Reed had his $5.6M deal fully guaranteed in the meantime.

Sit 3rd in the AL West with playoff hopes fading; called up top prospect Michael Arroyo and got 11 strikeouts over 7 innings from Logan Gilbert against Texas on Sept. 10 as the front office evaluates young talent down the stretch.

deepDive.title: Why a 10-Year Yield Near 5% Is a Valuation Problem, Not Just a Bond-Market Story
content: Today's brief has two numbers doing the real work: a hot core CPI print and a 10-year Treasury yield sitting at 4.97%, its highest level since 2023. It's tempting to treat the yield move as a fixed-income footnote while the headline S&P gain of 0.86% gets the attention. But the two are mechanically linked, and understanding how a rising discount rate reshapes equity valuations — even on a day stocks go up — is the more durable lesson than any single day's percentage move.

The 10-year yield is built from two pieces: the market's expected average path of short-term rates over the next decade, and a term premium investors demand as compensation for the extra risk of locking up money that long. Both pieces moved together this week. Thursday's hot PPI print pushed Fed hike odds higher, lifting the expected-rates component; Friday's CPI confirmed it, adding another 3 basis points. When both components rise in the same direction rather than offsetting each other, the yield move tends to be more persistent, because it reflects a genuine repricing of the macro outlook rather than a single day's positioning shift.

Here's what most people miss: equity valuations are built on discounted future cash flows, and the discount rate applied to those cash flows moves nearly one-for-one with long-term yields. A stock trading at 25 times next year's earnings is implicitly betting that today's low discount rate persists; when the 10-year climbs from 4.5% to 5% over a matter of weeks, as it's done since summer, the present value of a dollar earned in year ten falls meaningfully more than the present value of a dollar earned next year. That's why growth stocks with earnings concentrated far in the future — not value stocks with near-term cash flows — are historically the most sensitive to this exact kind of yield move, even when the headline index looks fine.

That's also the tension sitting underneath today's rally: the S&P and Nasdaq-100 both rose because oil eased and Oracle's cloud beat reassured investors that AI-driven demand is real, not because the yield backdrop improved. If the Fed does hike next week as futures now imply, watch whether the 10-year yield actually breaks above 5% or instead stalls out on the news — a classic 'sell the rumor, buy the fact' pattern where the repricing has already happened. Either way, the next CPI print and the Fed's own dot plot next week will matter more for where equity valuations settle than any single day's headline move.
